families.title: Bridge Courier islands
families.mathematics: A walk that crosses every bridge of a town exactly once leaves each island it passes through by a different bridge from the one it came in on, so every island in the middle of the walk uses its bridges in pairs; only the two ends can have an odd number of bridges. Euler (1736) showed the converse for a town in one piece: a walk over every bridge exactly once exists exactly when zero or two islands have an odd number of bridges. With zero it can start anywhere and comes back; with two it runs from one of them to the other. Königsberg has four odd islands, so no walk; the fewest new bridges for a walk that comes back is half the number of odd islands, since each odd island needs a new bridge end and a bridge has two. A delivery route that must come back may repeat bridges instead; then a repeat runs along existing bridges, so the fewest repeats can exceed half the odd islands: the three-arm star needs 3, one for each dead end, not 2 (the Chinese postman problem).
rules: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter.
Two islands can be joined by more than one bridge.

sources.title: Bellingham Math Circle — Week 10: Bridges and one-stroke drawings, student packets (K–1, 2–3, 4–5) and adult guide
L. Euler — Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis (1736): the seven bridges of Königsberg
J. Edmonds and E. L. Johnson — Matching, Euler tours and the Chinese postman, Mathematical Programming 5 (1973): routes that repeat as little as possible

puzzles.title: Three bridges
puzzles.objective: Color every island where a walk that picks up every counter can start.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Color every island where a walk that picks up every counter can start.
puzzles.instruction: Color every island where a walk that picks up every counter can start.
puzzles.controls: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter; a bridge without its counter can’t be crossed. Tap an island to put the token there, then tap a bridge, or the island across it, to cross. Again lifts the token and puts every counter back; Undo takes back one step. A walk that picks up every counter colours the island it started on, and Color colours or uncolours an island by hand. When every island where such a walk can start is coloured, press Done. If no walk can pick up every counter, try one, then press No walk, tap every island a walk would have to start or end on, and press Check.
rules: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter.
Two islands can be joined by more than one bridge.
A bridge without its counter can’t be crossed.
puzzles.idea: With three bridges between two islands, each walk over all three starts on one island and ends on the other, so both are starts.
puzzles.prerequisites: None; the counters show what is left.
hints: Try a walk from each island.
A walk from A crosses to B, back to A and to B again.
Both islands work.

parent.notice: Whether your child checks the second island, or stops after one walk.
parent.prompt: Where did your walk end? Could a walk start there?
parent.explanation: A has three bridges and so does B. A walk from A goes A, B, A, B; turned around it starts from B. Both islands are starts, and every walk ends on the other one.
parent.extension: What if there were four bridges?
parent.connection: Two places joined by several roads form a multigraph; Euler’s Königsberg had two double bridges.

puzzles.provenance: Week 10 K–1 Problem 3, town 2 (two islands joined by three bridges), asked as Problem 2’s question.

puzzles.idea: A walk from A crosses the two A–B bridges and comes back to A before it can reach C; so A is no start, while B and C are.
hints: Try a walk from each island. Which walks get stuck?
A walk from A comes back to A with C’s bridge left over.
Color B and C.

parent.notice: Whether your child predicts that starting at the end of the row works.
parent.prompt: Your walk from A got stuck. Where was the token, and which counter was left?
parent.explanation: A has two bridges, B three and C one. A walk from A uses both A–B bridges and is back at A with C’s counter left. From B: B, A, B, C. From C: C, B, A, B. Only the islands with an odd number of bridges work.
parent.extension: Add a second bridge to C. Where can a walk start now?
parent.connection: A walk over every bridge starts and ends on the islands with an odd number of bridges (Euler).

puzzles.provenance: Week 10 K–1 Problem 4, town 2 (a double bridge then a single one), asked as Problem 2’s question.

puzzles.title: Star
puzzles.objective: Add one bridge, then pick up every counter.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Add one bridge, then pick up every counter.
puzzles.instruction: Add one bridge, then pick up every counter.
puzzles.controls: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter; a bridge without its counter can’t be crossed. With Bridge, tap two islands to build a new bridge between them, or tap a new bridge to take it away. Then, with Walk: Tap an island to put the token there, then tap a bridge, or the island across it, to cross. Again lifts the token and puts every counter back; Undo takes back one step.
rules: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter.
Two islands can be joined by more than one bridge.
A bridge without its counter can’t be crossed.
puzzles.idea: No walk crosses all three bridges of a star: two of its three dead ends would both have to be ends of the walk and the third too. One new bridge between any two islands removes the trouble.
hints: Walk first: where do you get stuck?
A new bridge between two dead ends lets a walk go through them.
Add a bridge from A to C, then walk from B.

parent.notice: Whether your child walks first to find the problem, or adds a bridge at random.
parent.prompt: Which island did your walk get stuck on? Which counters were left?
parent.explanation: A, C and D each have one bridge, so a walk can only begin or end at each; a walk has two ends, so one counter is always left. Any new bridge joins two of the four islands with an odd number of bridges, leaving two, and then a walk runs from one to the other.
parent.extension: Can you add the new bridge so that the walk ends where it started? (No: two islands still have an odd number of bridges.)
parent.connection: Adding an edge between two odd vertices leaves two, and the graph gains an Euler trail.

puzzles.provenance: Week 10 K–1 Problem 6 and grades 2–3 Problem 4, town 1 (the three-arm star).

rules: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter.
Two islands can be joined by more than one bridge.
A bridge without its counter can’t be crossed.
puzzles.idea: Every island has an even number of bridges, so a walk over every bridge can start anywhere, and it comes back.
hints: Try a walk from a corner, then from the middle.
A walk from A that goes round both squares comes back to A.
Every island works.

parent.notice: Whether your child expects the corners and the middle to behave differently.
parent.prompt: Where did the walk end? What if you start from where it ended?
parent.explanation: The corners have two bridges and B and E four. A walk A, B, C, F, E, B, E, D, A crosses all eight and is back at A; it is a loop, so it can be started anywhere along it. All six islands are starts.
parent.extension: Take away one of the B–E bridges. Where can a walk start now?
parent.connection: With every degree even, an Euler circuit exists and passes through every vertex, so every vertex is a start (Euler; Hierholzer).

puzzles.provenance: Week 10 K–1 Problem 4, town 3 (two squares with a doubled middle rung), asked as Problem 2’s question.

puzzles.idea: Four islands have an odd number of bridges (D has five, A, C and F one), and a walk has only two ends, so there is no walk. The child taps those four.
hints: Try a few walks. Where do they get stuck?
A, C and F each have one bridge: a walk can only begin or end there.
Press No walk, tap A, C, D and F, and Check.

parent.notice: Whether your child keeps trying walks, or starts to argue that none can work.
parent.prompt: Which islands can a walk only start or end on?
parent.explanation: A, C and F have one bridge each, so a walk must begin or end there; D has five. Four islands with an odd number of bridges would need four ends, and a walk has two. So no walk picks up every counter.
parent.extension: Which one bridge could you add to make a walk possible?
parent.connection: More than two odd vertices: no Euler trail (Euler, 1736).

puzzles.title: Ladder with a crossing
puzzles.objective: Color every island where a walk that picks up every counter can start.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Color every island where a walk that picks up every counter can start.
puzzles.instruction: Color every island where a walk that picks up every counter can start.
puzzles.controls: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter; a bridge without its counter can’t be crossed. Tap an island to put the token there, then tap a bridge, or the island across it, to cross. Again lifts the token and puts every counter back; Undo takes back one step. A walk that picks up every counter colours the island it started on, and Color colours or uncolours an island by hand. When every island where such a walk can start is coloured, press Done. If no walk can pick up every counter, try one, then press No walk, tap every island a walk would have to start or end on, and press Check.
rules: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter.
Two islands can be joined by more than one bridge.
A bridge without its counter can’t be crossed.
puzzles.idea: Only D and F have an odd number of bridges (three each), so every walk over every bridge runs from one to the other; B, with the most bridges, is no start.
hints: Try a walk from B, the island with the most bridges.
Walks from B get stuck; try the bottom corners.
Color D and F.

parent.notice: Whether your child expects the busiest island to be the best start.
parent.prompt: Your walk ended on F. Could a walk start there?
parent.explanation: D and F have three bridges, B four, the rest two. A walk D, A, B, D, E, F, B, C, F crosses all eight; reversed it starts from F. From any other island the walk would have to end there too, leaving D and F each with a bridge unused.
parent.extension: Which bridge could you take away so that a walk can start anywhere?
parent.connection: Exactly two odd vertices: every Euler trail runs between them.

puzzles.provenance: Week 10 grades 2–3 Problem 2, town 3 (the ladder ring with two diagonals from the top middle).

puzzles.title: Square with a cross
puzzles.objective: Add one bridge, then pick up every counter.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Add one bridge, then pick up every counter.
puzzles.instruction: Add one bridge, then pick up every counter.
puzzles.controls: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter; a bridge without its counter can’t be crossed. With Bridge, tap two islands to build a new bridge between them, or tap a new bridge to take it away. Then, with Walk: Tap an island to put the token there, then tap a bridge, or the island across it, to cross. Again lifts the token and puts every counter back; Undo takes back one step.
rules: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter.
Two islands can be joined by more than one bridge.
A bridge without its counter can’t be crossed.
puzzles.idea: The four corners have three bridges each. A new bridge between two corners leaves two odd islands and a walk; a new bridge to the middle island leaves four, and still no walk.
hints: Walk first: where do you get stuck?
A new bridge to the middle island doesn’t help. Join two corners.
Add a bridge from A to B, then walk from D.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries the middle island first, and what they make of it not working.
parent.prompt: Which islands can a walk only start or end on?
parent.explanation: Corners have three bridges, the middle four. A new bridge between two corners makes both even and leaves the other two corners as the ends of a walk. A new bridge from a corner to the middle makes the middle odd, so four odd islands remain. Six of the ten possible new bridges work.
parent.extension: Can a new bridge make a walk that ends where it started?
parent.connection: An edge changes the parity of exactly its two ends.

puzzles.provenance: Week 10 K–1 Problem 6, town 2 (a square with both diagonals through a middle island).

puzzles.title: House
puzzles.objective: Add as few bridges as you can, then pick up every counter and end where you started.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Add as few bridges as you can, then pick up every counter and end where you started.
puzzles.instruction: Add as few bridges as you can, then pick up every counter and end where you started.
puzzles.controls: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter; a bridge without its counter can’t be crossed. With Bridge, tap two islands to build a new bridge between them, or tap a new bridge to take it away. With Walk: Tap an island to put the token there, then tap a bridge, or the island across it, to cross. Again lifts the token and puts every counter back; Undo takes back one step. When your walk has picked up every counter and is back where it started, press Fewest if no smaller number of new bridges could work, tap every island that needs a new bridge, and press Check.
rules: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter.
Two islands can be joined by more than one bridge.
A bridge without its counter can’t be crossed.
puzzles.idea: B and C have three bridges, so a walk that comes back needs a new bridge at each; one new bridge from B to C reaches both.
hints: Can you walk it from one island and come back? Where do your walks end?
B and C each need a new bridge.
Add a bridge from B to C, then walk from A.

parent.notice: Whether your child adds bridges until it works, then tries to do with fewer.
parent.prompt: Your walk ended on C, not where it started. What would fix that?
parent.explanation: B and C have three bridges each and the rest two. A walk that comes back uses every island’s bridges in pairs, so B and C each need one more bridge; a single new B–C bridge gives both. Then A, B, D, E, C, B, C, A crosses all seven.
parent.extension: With the new bridge in place, where can the walk start?
parent.connection: A closed walk over every edge (an Euler circuit) needs every degree even.

puzzles.objective: Color every island where a walk that picks up every counter can start.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Color every island where a walk that picks up every counter can start.
puzzles.instruction: Color every island where a walk that picks up every counter can start.
puzzles.controls: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter; a bridge without its counter can’t be crossed. Tap an island to put the token there, then tap a bridge, or the island across it, to cross. Again lifts the token and puts every counter back; Undo takes back one step. A walk that picks up every counter colours the island it started on, and Color colours or uncolours an island by hand. When every island where such a walk can start is coloured, press Done. If no walk can pick up every counter, try one, then press No walk, tap every island a walk would have to start or end on, and press Check.
rules: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter.
Two islands can be joined by more than one bridge.
A bridge without its counter can’t be crossed.
puzzles.idea: All four land areas of Königsberg have an odd number of bridges (5, 3, 3 and 3), so no walk crosses every bridge once: Euler’s proof.
hints: Try a few walks. Which islands do they get stuck on?
Every island here has an odd number of bridges.
Press No walk, tap A, B, C and D, and Check.

parent.notice: Whether your child counts bridges after a few walks, or keeps walking.
parent.prompt: How many bridges does each land area have? Which could be the ends of a walk?
parent.explanation: A has five bridges and B, C and D three each. An island in the middle of a walk is entered and left in pairs, so each odd island must be an end of the walk, and a walk has two ends. Four odd islands: no walk. This is Euler’s 1736 solution.
parent.extension: Where could the city build one new bridge so that a walk exists?
parent.connection: Euler’s Königsberg paper is often counted as the first theorem of graph theory.

puzzles.provenance: Week 10 grades 4–5 Problem 5 (Königsberg, with its double bridges), asked as Problem 2’s question.

puzzles.title: Königsberg comes back
puzzles.objective: Add as few bridges as you can, then pick up every counter and end where you started.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Add as few bridges as you can, then pick up every counter and end where you started.
puzzles.instruction: Add as few bridges as you can, then pick up every counter and end where you started.
puzzles.controls: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter; a bridge without its counter can’t be crossed. With Bridge, tap two islands to build a new bridge between them, or tap a new bridge to take it away. With Walk: Tap an island to put the token there, then tap a bridge, or the island across it, to cross. Again lifts the token and puts every counter back; Undo takes back one step. When your walk has picked up every counter and is back where it started, press Fewest if no smaller number of new bridges could work, tap every island that needs a new bridge, and press Check.
rules: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter.
Two islands can be joined by more than one bridge.
A bridge without its counter can’t be crossed.
puzzles.idea: Four odd islands each need a new bridge end, and a bridge has two, so two new bridges (pairing the four in any way) are the fewest for a walk that comes back.
hints: Walk first. Which islands do your walks get stuck on?
Each island with an odd number of bridges needs one new bridge.
Add bridges from A to B and from C to D, then walk.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries one new bridge first and sees why it can’t be enough.
parent.prompt: After one new bridge, how many islands still have an odd number?
parent.explanation: A, B, C and D are all odd. A walk that comes back needs every island even, so each needs a new bridge end; a bridge has two ends, so at least two bridges, and A–B with C–D (or A–C with B–D, or A–D with B–C) does it.
parent.extension: For a walk that may end anywhere, how many new bridges are needed? (One.)
parent.connection: Making a graph Eulerian with fewest added edges: pair the odd vertices.

puzzles.provenance: Week 10 grades 4–5 Problem 5, last question (the fewest new bridges for a walk that ends where it started).

puzzles.title: Star delivery
puzzles.objective: Pick up every counter and end where you started, crossing bridges again as few times as you can.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Pick up every counter and end where you started, crossing bridges again as few times as you can.
puzzles.instruction: Pick up every counter and end where you started, crossing bridges again as few times as you can.
puzzles.controls: A route starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter. A bridge can be crossed again after its counter is gone; each crossing after the first is a repeat, and the bridge shows how many times it was crossed. Tap an island to put the token there, then tap a bridge, or the island across it, to cross. Again lifts the token and puts every counter back; Undo takes back one step. When the route has picked up every counter and is back where it started, press Fewest if no route could repeat less, tap every dead end, and press Check.
rules: A walk starts on an island and crosses bridges one after another, picking up each bridge’s counter.
Two islands can be joined by more than one bridge.
A bridge can be crossed again after its counter is gone; each crossing after the first is a repeat.
puzzles.idea: A route that comes back must leave each dead end along the bridge it came in on, so all three bridges are crossed twice: 3 repeats, not the 2 that half the four odd islands suggests.
hints: Try a route. Which bridges did you cross twice?
A route into a dead end must come back out over the same bridge.
From B: to A and back, to C and back, to D and back. Then Fewest, tap A, C and D, and Check.

parent.notice: Whether your child expects 2 repeats, as two new bridges would fix four odd islands, and what they make of needing 3.
parent.prompt: How does a route leave a dead end?
parent.explanation: Each of A, C and D has one bridge, so a route that visits it and comes back crosses that bridge twice. That is three repeats whichever island the route starts on, and B, A, B, C, B, D, B uses exactly three. New bridges could go anywhere; repeats must run along existing bridges, which is why the count is 3, not 2.
parent.extension: For a route that may end anywhere, what is the fewest? (Two: start on one dead end and finish on another.)
parent.connection: The Chinese postman problem: the fewest repeats pair the odd vertices along shortest paths (Edmonds and Johnson, 1973).

puzzles.provenance: Week 10 grades 4–5 Problems 10–11, town 2 (the three-arm star as a delivery route).
